title: How the SAT Is Built and Scored

beats.say: The SAT is a standardized test that many colleges use when they make admissions decisions. You take it on a laptop or tablet, in an app called Bluebook, at a test center.
The test has two sections. One is Reading and Writing, and the other is Math. Each section gets its own score, and colleges see both scores.
Each section is scored from two hundred to eight hundred. Added together, your total score falls anywhere from four hundred to sixteen hundred.

scenes.title: How the test is laid out

beats.say: Here's how the test is laid out. Reading and Writing has two modules, with twenty-seven questions in each, so fifty-four questions in total. Each module lasts thirty-two minutes.
Math also has two modules, with twenty-two questions in each, so forty-four in total. Each Math module lasts thirty-five minutes.
A ten minute break separates the two sections. Altogether, the test takes about two hours and fourteen minutes.
The SAT is adaptive by module. That means how you do on the first module of a section decides how hard the second module of that section will be.
The harder second module is the only way to reach the top scores. So your answers in the first module matter twice: they count, and they shape what comes next.

card.sub: the path to the top scores

beats.say: Inside a module, you are free to move back and forth, flag questions, and change your answers, right up until the time for that module runs out.
Each Reading and Writing question has one short passage, sometimes two, or a table or chart, followed by a single question. These questions test four areas.
The second area is Craft and Structure. These questions ask how words and paragraphs work inside a text.
The third area is Expression of Ideas. These questions ask whether a text says what it wants to say in the best way.
The fourth area is Standard English Conventions, which covers punctuation, sentence structure, and grammar. The units in this course follow exactly these four areas.
Math is mostly multiple choice, but about one quarter of the questions ask you to type in your own answer. Math also has four areas. The first is Algebra.
The second area is Advanced Math, which includes quadratics, exponentials, and other nonlinear functions.
The third area is Problem-Solving and Data Analysis, which covers ratios, percentages, statistics, and probability.
The fourth area is Geometry and Trigonometry, which covers area, volume, angles, circles, and right triangles.
In the Math section, the test includes a built-in Desmos graphing calculator. This course teaches Desmos step by step, so you'll be comfortable using it.
You also get a reference sheet with common formulas, so you don't have to memorize every single one.
There's no penalty for wrong answers, so never leave a question blank. If you are stuck, make your best guess, flag the question, and come back if time allows.
Don't get stuck. Five minutes on one hard question can cost you two easier questions later in the module. Guess, flag it, and move on.
beats.item: Do not get stuck on one question

beats.say: Pace yourself. Reading and Writing gives you about seventy-one seconds per question, and Math gives you about ninety-five seconds per question.
To recap. The SAT has two sections, Reading and Writing and Math, each scored from two hundred to eight hundred, for a total from four hundred to sixteen hundred.
Each section has two modules, and your first module decides how hard the second one will be.
Never leave a question blank. Guess, flag, and keep moving. In the next video, we look at how to study with OpenPrep.
